source.title: Predicting Emergent Capabilities by Finetuning
source.authors: Charles Burton Snell; Eric Wallace; Dan Klein; Sergey Levine

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present. The appendix includes unrelated coding-problem prompt and solution material, which is not evidence about the claim.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests downstream capability prediction against pretraining loss using an emergence-threshold model, rather than testing the original held-out pretraining-loss scaling laws or compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper cites the original pretraining-loss scaling laws as background but does not test them. Its own relevant results concern downstream benchmark accuracy and prediction of emergence points. Results cited from other work are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study tests whether downstream performance is predictable from pretraining loss. It predicts where few-shot emergence occurs from a finetuning-based emergence law fitted on small OpenLLaMA checkpoints, then checks against larger 7B/13B checkpoints. It does not test pretraining-loss scaling (V1–V3), shape (V4), other modalities (V5) or pretraining-law fit-dependence (V7).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that finetuning shifts the emergence point toward weaker models and that a fitted emergence law predicts few-shot emergence within 0.1 nats on four benchmarks. In some tasks it does so up to about 4x FLOPs in advance, far short of post-emergence forecasting. Pretraining loss serves as a size-independent variable for capability. Applications to data-quality comparison (OpenLLaMA V2 predicted to emerge before V1) and to APPS (about 325B parameters for LLaMA 2, unverifiable) are proof-of-concept.
record.recipe_differences: The study models downstream emergence with a ReLU performance curve and a parametric law for how the emergence point shifts with finetuning data. It does not reproduce the original pretraining-loss scaling-law or compute-optimal allocation method.
record.method_sensitivity: Prediction horizon varies by task. Prediction error is affected by the emergence-law functional form and by which finetuning subsets and checkpoints are used; the low-data limit has minimal impact within a reasonable range. Finetuning data amount changes the observed emergence shift.

fits_no_version.finding: Task-specific finetuning shifts the emergence elbow (as a function of pretraining loss) toward weaker models, and more finetuning data shifts it further. LoRA, even rank 1, shifts it comparably; prefix tuning and changing the number of shots do not.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Finetuning on a task moves the pretraining-loss point of emergence earlier, scaling with finetuning data amount; parameter updates appear necessary.

record.problems: The study uses selected model families and NLP benchmarks. The APPS prediction cannot be checked against a model beyond 70B. Some ablation results are presented graphically, and the authors report task-dependent prediction horizons and sensitivity to data/checkpoint selection.
record.rows_left_out: Individual finetuning runs across data fractions and intermediate checkpoints in Figures 3, 4, 14, 16, and 17 are not separately catalogued; relevant aggregate findings and prediction results are recorded in R13–R17. Table 2's many individual task-by-ablation entries are summarized in R17 rather than transcribed separately.

untested.parts: Smooth post-emergence extrapolation of downstream accuracy (the ReLU is not used to extrapolate the slope); tasks beyond four NLP benchmarks plus APPS; non-transformer architectures or distilled models (authors flag this); horizons far beyond about 4x FLOPs; APPS prediction accuracy (unverifiable).
No pretraining-loss sweep. The only loss-vs-parameter fit is a 4-point LLaMA 2 fit to losses read from Touvron et al., used as a conversion tool.
Not tested; finetuning is used as a probe, not as a scaling-law regime for loss.

missing.what: Emergence persists under a continuous probability-of-correct-answer metric on MMLU and CSQA. This bears on whether downstream non-smoothness is a metric artefact.
Prefix tuning and 0- vs 5-shot prompting give little or no emergence shift; LoRA rank 1–64 matches full finetuning.
MCMC vs bootstrap intervals are similar. The APPS bootstrap interval maps to 225B–830B parameters vs 244B–509B for MCMC.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. The LLaMA 2 loss-vs-parameter fit (L(N)=1.594·N^-0.089+0.408, 4 points from Touvron et al.) is used only as a tool to convert loss to parameters; it is not treated as a V1 test. On GSM8K three 3B checkpoints are technically post-emergence by ground truth (<3% accuracy). The MMLU setup finetunes on the test split and evaluates on validation.

versions.untested_parts: No sweep tests held-out pretraining loss against parameters, tokens, or compute.
Does not test whether power laws fitted to small pretraining runs predict the held-out loss of much larger runs.
Does not compare compute-optimal parameter and token allocations.
Does not vary architecture depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No tests of other modalities, repeated data, or transfer/fine-tuning scaling laws of the kind stated in this version.
The tests concern emergence on selected NLP benchmarks and one APPS case study, not general downstream performance across tasks or model families.

The paper varies fitting choices for its downstream emergence law, but does not test whether pretraining-loss scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocations depend on setup as stated in this version.

rows.subject: LLaMA 2
rows.stage_stated: base pretrained models; few-shot APPS evaluation
rows.operation_detail: Evaluate greedy pass@1 accuracy on APPS and describe these models as pre-emergence.
rows.note: These measurements establish that the tested LLaMA 2 models remain pre-emergence; they do not validate the later emergence prediction.
rows.check: Near-random APPS pass@1 (0.04%, 0.04%, 0.16%) from 7B to 70B shows flat pre-emergence performance. It is consistent with emergence but gives no test of the prediction.

rows.subject: OpenLLaMA V1 intermediate checkpoints
rows.operation_detail: Plot downstream benchmark performance against pretraining loss across intermediate checkpoints and model sizes.
rows.measure: Downstream performance and emergence point as a function of pretraining loss
rows.baseline: Random guessing is shown where reported
rows.value: Authors state that emergence points and subsequent downstream performance scaling versus pretraining loss are consistent across model sizes in both settings; for CoLA, full-data finetuning shifts the elbow before all considered checkpoints.
rows.locator: Appendix A.4, Figure 14; Appendix A.11, Figure 16
rows.note: Aggregate statement across tasks and model sizes; the CoLA full-data finetuning elbow is outside the observed checkpoint range.
rows.check: State should be observed, not partial. The authors state downstream-vs-loss curves and emergence points are consistent across 3B/7B/13B in both settings. The CoLA elbow falling before all checkpoints under full-data finetuning is a visibility issue, not a weaker effect.

rows.subject: OpenLLaMA V1 intermediate checkpoints
rows.operation_detail: Compare downstream performance against pretraining loss for few-shot and finetuned models.
rows.measure: Position of the emergence point as finetuning data amount changes
rows.value: Finetuning shifts the emergence point toward less capable models; increasing finetuning data shifts it further toward less capable models.
rows.note: This is a downstream emergence result, not a test of pretraining-loss scaling with training tokens or compute.
rows.check: Finetuning shifting the emergence elbow toward weaker models is the study's own finding about finetuning, not a measure of whether downstream performance scales predictably with scale or loss. Moved to fits_no_version.

rows.value: Finetuning shifts the emergence point toward less capable models; increasing finetuning data shifts it further toward less capable models.
rows.note: The paper also reports that the shift is consistent across model sizes at the same pretraining loss.
rows.check: Same as R14: a finetuning-shift finding, not a V6 measure. The cross-size consistency part is already covered by R13.

rows.subject: OpenLLaMA V1 intermediate checkpoints
rows.operation_detail: Compare emergence-law prediction error under different functional forms and low-data extrapolation limits.

conditions.value: Log power law versus power law; varying D0

rows.value: The log power law generally gives the best predictions; changing D0 within a reasonable range (less than 10N) has minimal impact; adding the few-shot adjustment has an overall small effect.
rows.uncertainty: Figure 6 error bars show 5th and 95th percentile errors from MCMC posterior sampling
rows.note: The paper reports aggregate conclusions across the four tasks; exact values are presented graphically.
rows.check: This is an ablation of the study's own method variants (log power law vs power law, D0, Δ), not a direct measure of downstream predictability. Keep it only as context on robustness; per Figure 6, the alternative forms still mostly predict within about 0.1 nats.

rows.value: Smaller finetuning subsets are often more important for accurate predictions; using only one subsample can worsen predictions; removing checkpoints can worsen predictions, though some well-spaced three-checkpoint fits remain accurate.
rows.uncertainty: Table 2 reports 5th and 95th percentile prediction errors from MCMC posterior sampling

relationships.condition: OpenLLaMA V1 3B-fitted predictions of few-shot emergence on GSM8K, MMLU, CSQA, CoLA; V1/V2 on MMLU with C4 loss
relationships.reason: MLE emergence points fall within 0.1 nats of ground truth on all tasks (R1–R4, R9, R10). Downstream-vs-loss curves coincide across 3B/7B/13B (R13).
relationships.display_finding: Estimated emergence thresholds were within 0.1 nats of ground truth on all tasks, and downstream performance curves aligned across 3B, 7B, and 13B when plotted against loss.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: OpenLLaMA V1 3B-fitted predictions of few-shot emergence on GSM8K, MMLU, CSQA, CoLA; V1/V2 on MMLU with C4 loss
source_check.reason: Table 3 confirms every listed MLE prediction is within 0.1 nats of ground truth; Appendix A.4 reports consistent downstream-versus-loss curves across model sizes.

relationships.reason: Successful advance prediction reaches only 4.3x/3.9x FLOPs (MMLU/GSM8K) and 1.9x/2.3x (CSQA/CoLA) (R5–R8). The authors contrast this with the 1000x reported for post-emergence prediction.
relationships.display_finding: Successful forecasts reached 4.3× FLOPs for MMLU, 3.9× for GSM8K, 1.9× for CSQA and 2.3× for CoLA, versus the reported 1000× after emergence.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: Section 6.4 and Figure 7 demonstrate task-dependent prediction horizons and failures with earlier checkpoints: 4.3x, 3.9x, 1.9x and 2.3x FLOPs.

relationships.condition: Few-shot downstream performance in the pre-emergence regime (incl. continuous metrics, APPS up to 70B)
relationships.reason: Few-shot accuracy sits at random until an elbow, so it is not a smooth function of scale. APPS stays near random through 70B (R11). Per the text (Fig. 13), emergence persists with a continuous log-prob metric on MMLU/CSQA; no row records this.
relationships.display_finding: Few-shot accuracy remained near random before an elbow, including APPS through 70B, while MMLU and CSQA still exhibited emergence under continuous log-probability metrics.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Few-shot downstream performance in the pre-emergence regime (incl. continuous metrics, APPS up to 70B)
source_check.reason: V6 requires predictability, not smooth improvement. Flat pre-emergence scores and emergence under continuous metrics do not establish prediction failure. R11 cannot determine predictability, and Section 7.2 explicitly leaves APPS forecast accuracy unvalidated.

relationships.condition: Choice of checkpoints and finetuning subsets used for fitting
relationships.reason: Dropping the smallest subsets, using a single subsample or fewer checkpoints often pushes error past 0.1 nats. Example: CSQA -3 smallest subsets, error 0.988 (R17).
relationships.display_finding: Reducing fitting subsets or checkpoints often raised prediction error above 0.1 nats, reaching 0.988 on CSQA after removing the three smallest subsets.
